section: Who this applies to
wording: - **The German payer.** A German company paying dividends, the German bank or custodian paying dividends on shares held in collective custody, or a German business paying royalties or certain interest to a non-resident. The payer withholds and pays the tax over. It is liable for tax it should have withheld (§ 44(5), § 50a(5) EStG).

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **The foreign recipient.** A person or company with neither residence nor management in Germany. It carries the tax, and claims the treaty or directive relief from the Bundeszentralamt für Steuern (BZSt), not from the payer.

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Withholding comes first.** The payer withholds the full domestic rate even when a treaty or directive limits German tax, unless the recipient holds an exemption certificate from the BZSt (§ 50c(1), (2) EStG). The payer cannot rely on the recipient's treaty rights itself.

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Dividends** from a company with its seat or management in Germany (§ 49(1) no. 5(a); § 43(1) no. 1 EStG).

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Interest.** Ordinary interest on a loan, bank account or listed bond paid to a non-resident is not German-source income and has no German tax (see de-non-resident-tax). Interest on convertible bonds, profit-sharing bonds (Gewinnobligationen) and profit-participation rights carries Kapitalertragsteuer (§ 43(1) no. 2). Loans secured on German land are German-source income too (§ 49(1) no. 5(c)). So a treaty interest rate matters only for these cases.

section: Who this applies to
wording: - **Royalties** for the use of rights, know-how, plans or processes, used in Germany (§ 50a(1) no. 3; § 49(1) nos. 2, 3, 6, 9 EStG).

section: Treaty limits on German tax, by country of the recipient
wording: Profit-dependent income needs care. Several treaties let Germany tax income from a silent partnership, a profit-participating loan or profit-sharing bonds at its domestic rate where the payer can deduct it: for example Austria art. 11(2), France art. 9(9), Ireland protocol no. 3, Netherlands protocol no. IX, US art. 10(6). Switzerland caps it at 30% instead of 15% (art. 10(2)(b)). Read the treaty before applying a 0% interest rate to such income.

section: Step 1: what is withheld
wording: 1. **Dividends.** 25% Kapitalertragsteuer on the gross dividend, plus 5.5% surcharge on that tax: 26.375% (§ 43a(1), (2) EStG). The full gross is the base; no costs are deducted. The tax arises on the day the dividend is paid as fixed in the distribution resolution (§ 44(2)). The company withholds; for shares in collective custody, the German custodian bank does (§ 44(1) sentence 3).

section: Step 1: what is withheld
wording: 2. **Profit-dependent interest.** The same 26.375% (§ 43(1) no. 2, § 43a(1) no. 1).

section: Step 1: what is withheld
wording: 3. **Royalties.** 15% of gross receipts plus surcharge: 15.825% (§ 50a(2)). Costs can be deducted only for the receipts listed in § 50a(3), which does not include royalties.

section: Step 2: what the recipient can get back
wording: **Portfolio holdings below 15% (§ 50j).** Where a treaty cuts German tax on dividends below 15% for a shareholder that is not a company holding at least 10% (for example the US pension fund at 0%, or the Dutch pension fund and UK pension scheme at 10%), the refund needs the recipient to have been the beneficial owner for 45 days within 45 days either side of the due date, carrying at least 70% of the risk of a fall in value, and not to pass the dividend on (§ 50j EStG). The tests in § 50j(1)–(3) do not apply if, at receipt, the recipient has been the economic owner of the shares or participation certificates continuously for at least one year (§ 50j(4) sentence 2); the FIFO rule in § 50j(2) sentence 2 still applies.
evidence_note: DE-L17: actual50j(4)sentence2 one-year continuous-ownership exception must accompany45day/70percent conditions; root correction applied; exact98b7a3ed successor bound.

section: Step 2: what the recipient can get back
wording: § 50g does not cover interest treated as a profit distribution, interest on profit-participating claims, or the part of interest or royalties above an arm's length amount (§ 50g(2)).

section: Step 2: what the recipient can get back
wording: **Refund amount on a treaty dividend.** Refund = tax withheld − treaty limit × gross dividend. For a 15% treaty: 26.375% − 15% = 11.375% of the gross. This holds where the treaty's covered taxes include the solidarity surcharge. Austria, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Spain, the UK, Ireland and Poland list German taxes "including the supplements levied thereon" (art. 2); Switzerland and France cover taxes levied "also in the form of surcharges" (art. 2(1), art. 1(2)). Italy and the US do not expressly name supplements; their later-similar-tax clauses are Italy art. 2(4) and US art. 2(2). Czech Republic art. 2(3)(a) expressly names the corporation-tax Ergänzungsabgabe; whether the current solidarity surcharge falls within that wording or the later-similar-tax clause in art. 2(5) is not separately established here.
evidence_note: DE-L18: Czech2(3)(a)actually names historic corporation-taxErgaenzungsabgabe; current solidarity-surcharge coverage remains precise unresolved question, not inferred solely from old levy name.

section: Step 3: the anti-treaty-shopping test (§ 50d(3) EStG)
wording: A foreign company gets no treaty relief from Kapitalertragsteuer or § 50a tax to the extent that:

section: Step 3: the anti-treaty-shopping test (§ 50d(3) EStG)
wording: 1. its shareholders or beneficiaries would not have the relief if they earned the income directly, and

section: Step 3: the anti-treaty-shopping test (§ 50d(3) EStG)
wording: 2. the income has no substantial link to the company's own business. Earning the income and passing it on, and activity carried on with a business not set up adequately for its purpose, are not business.

section: Step 3: the anti-treaty-shopping test (§ 50d(3) EStG)
wording: The company escapes if it shows that none of the main purposes of its involvement is a tax advantage, or if its main class of shares is traded substantially and regularly on a recognised exchange. § 43b, § 50g and § 44a(9) apply § 50d(3) too. § 42 AO (abuse) still applies.

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **Payer liability.** The payer is liable for Kapitalertragsteuer it should have withheld, unless it shows it did not breach its duties deliberately or with gross negligence (§ 44(5)). For § 50a tax the payer is liable without that defence; the recipient can also be pursued (§ 50a(5) sentences 5, 6).

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **Late payment (§ 240 AO).** 1% per started month on tax not paid over on time, rounded down to EUR 50.

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **Late filing of a withholding return (§ 152(1) AO).** The tax office may set a late-filing surcharge. The amount for withholding returns is not set out here.

section: Penalties and interest
wording: - **Interest on § 50g refunds (§ 50c(4)).** 0.5% per full month (§ 238(1) AO; the 0.15% rate in § 238(1a) is only for § 233a interest), from 12 months after the month in which the complete application and evidence arrive, at the earliest from payment of the tax, until the refund decision takes effect. Treaty refunds carry no interest under § 50c(4).

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **The recipient's home country.** The tax that stays in Germany at the treaty rate is credited or relieved under the recipient's own law and the treaty's article on eliminating double tax. Not covered here.

wording: - **Non-cooperative jurisdictions.** Since 2022 the Tax Haven Defence Act (StAbwG § 10) brings further payments to residents of listed non-cooperative jurisdictions into withholding (BZSt notice). Not set out here.

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **German permanent establishment.** If the shares, claim or right belong to a German permanent establishment of the recipient, the treaty article on business profits applies instead and the income is assessed (for example Austria art. 10(4)).

section: Cross-border points
wording: - **Investment funds and REITs.** Several treaties limit the reduced dividend rate for REIT-AGs and investment funds (Switzerland, Netherlands, Ireland, Spain, Luxembourg, US). Check the treaty text.
